source.title: Open problems in queueing theory inspired by datacenter computing

accepted.question_text: Consider the multiserver job queueing model with n servers, First-Come-First-Served scheduling, and classes of jobs where a class-i job simultaneously requests n_i servers and holds them for a service duration S_i. Even in the simplified case where all jobs have the same exponentially distributed service durations, what is the mean response time for systems with more than n = 2 servers?

evidence.quote: In summary, understanding the mean response time for multiserver job systems with more than n = 2 servers is an entirely open problem, even when all jobs have the same exponentially distributed service durations.

accepted.question_text: In the multiserver job model, where jobs may request different numbers of servers and may have different service-time distributions, what is the exact stability region beyond the currently understood special cases such as identical exponential durations or the two-class exponential case?

evidence.quote: Very recently, Grosof et al. [82] derived a simple closed-form expression for the stability region of the multiserver job model where jobs have different exponential service time durations. Unfortunately, the work in [82] is limited to the case of only two classes. Characterizing the stability region in a more general setting is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: For the multiserver job model with a finite but nonzero waiting room, rather than either immediate service or immediate dropping, what performance results can be proved when jobs that cannot start service immediately may queue up to a finite capacity?

evidence.quote: An interesting open problem is whether anything can be said for the multiserver job model where there is a finite (but nonzero) queue capacity.

accepted.question_text: Suppose jobs arrive over time to a system with a fixed number n of servers, all jobs share the same concave, sublinear speedup function s(k), and each job's inherent size is unknown at arrival but is drawn from a non-exponential distribution. What server-allocation policy minimizes mean response time in this setting?

evidence.quote: If we consider the same setting as in [34], but where the inherent job size distribution is not exponential, then finding the optimal server allocation policy is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: Assume all jobs follow the same speedup function, but their inherent sizes are known when they are scheduled. What allocation policy minimizes mean response time in this known-size parallel scheduling setting?

evidence.quote: In this section, we continue to assume that all jobs follow the same speedup function, but now we assume that the inherent job sizes are all known. Optimizing mean response time in this setting is still a largely open problem.

accepted.question_text: When all jobs are present at time 0 and share a common speedup function that is neither of the form s(k)=k^p nor a simple threshold-based speedup function, what is the optimal way to allocate the n servers across jobs to minimize mean response time or mean slowdown?

evidence.quote: However if the speedup function is any non-trivial function other than s(k) = k^p or the simple threshold-based function, then it is an entirely open problem to determine how to optimally allocate servers to jobs.

accepted.question_text: When jobs with partially parallelizable speedup functions arrive over time, even for simple speedup models such as threshold-based speedup, what online allocation policy is optimal?

evidence.quote: Even for the simplest speedup functions (for example, threshold-based speedup), once we add in arrivals, the optimal allocation is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: Suppose there are two classes of jobs with strictly ranked speedup functions, all job sizes are unknown but are independently drawn from the same exponential distribution, and the scheduler must allocate servers to maximize performance. What allocation policy minimizes mean response time in this two-speedup-function setting?

evidence.quote: Even in the simplest case described above, where there are only two strictly ranked speedup functions, and where all jobs have inherent sizes drawn from the same exponential distribution, finding the optimal allocation policy is still an open problem.

accepted.question_text: When there are many job types, each with its own speedup function and its own distribution of inherent size, how should servers be allocated across jobs over time?

evidence.quote: In general, it is common that one has many types of jobs, each with a different speedup function and each with a different distribution of inherent size. It is a huge open problem to figure out how to allocate servers to jobs in this setting.

accepted.question_text: For a system where directed-acyclic-graph jobs arrive over time, each job consists of tasks with precedence constraints, and the scheduler must choose both which jobs to run and which tasks within each job to run on n servers, what is the optimal allocation policy for minimizing mean job response time?

evidence.quote: Even with these simplifications, finding the optimal allocation policy is a very hard open problem

accepted.question_text: For DAG-job scheduling policies in which jobs arrive over time and each job is complete only when all tasks in its DAG are complete, how can one analyze the mean job response time of a given allocation policy?

evidence.quote: analyzing the mean job response time of different allocation policies is also a hard open problem.

accepted.question_text: In the limited fork-join model with n distributed queues and jobs that create only k much smaller than n tasks, how large can k grow while the queues still exhibit asymptotic independence as n tends to infinity?

evidence.quote: While good progress has been made on analyzing the limited fork-join model, open problems remain. It is unclear how much larger k can be made while still achieving asymptotic independence.

accepted.question_text: In the limited fork-join model, what is the mean job response time when each arriving job dispatches its k tasks to the k shortest queues, or to the k queues with the least work, rather than to random queues?

evidence.quote: Analyzing the case where the k tasks are dispatched to the k shortest queues, or k queues with least work is also an interesting open problem

accepted.question_text: For the stochastic M/G/k queue with arrivals over time, outside the heavy-traffic regime typical optimality results do not apply. Under what conditions is SRPT-k actually optimal for minimizing mean response time?

evidence.quote: Outside of heavy traffic, understanding when SRPT-k is optimal and analyzing its performance are both big open problems.

accepted.question_text: For the stochastic M/G/k queue with arrivals over time, what is the mean-response-time performance of SRPT-k outside the heavy-traffic regime?

evidence.quote: Outside of heavy traffic, understanding when SRPT-k is optimal and analyzing its performance are both big open problems.

accepted.question_text: In a distributed load-balancing system with multiple server queues and SRPT scheduling within each server, what dispatching policy minimizes mean response time outside the heavy-traffic limit?

evidence.quote: Outside of heavy traffic, optimal dispatching is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: In the single-server M/G/1 setting with unknown job sizes, can the known factor-5 guarantee for a simple policy relative to the optimal Gittins policy be improved, or can other simple policies be found that achieve comparably near-optimal mean response time?

evidence.quote: In [130], Scully et al. proved that a much simpler policy, related to SERPT, is within a factor 5 of optimal. It is an open problem whether that factor can be improved, or whether other simple policies with near-optimal mean response time exist.

accepted.question_text: For the multi-server M/G/k queue when job sizes are not known a priori and the Gittins rank policy is extended to run the k jobs with lowest Gittins ranks, is Gittins-k optimal outside of heavy traffic?

evidence.quote: Proving the optimality of Gittins-k outside of heavy traffic remains an open problem.

accepted.question_text: Suppose every arriving job has a hard deadline of 400 ms and the objective is to minimize the fraction of jobs whose response time exceeds that deadline. What scheduling policy minimizes P{Response time > 400 ms}?

evidence.quote: How to schedule jobs to minimize P {Response time > 400 ms} is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: For the Drop-The-Larger-Hopeless policy, which keeps First-Come-First-Served queue order except that on an infeasible arrival it may drop a larger queued job instead of the new smaller job, how close is this policy to the true optimum for minimizing deadline misses?

evidence.quote: While DTLH sounds good, it too is not optimal, and it is an open problem to determine how close to optimal it is.

accepted.question_text: For the Drop-The-Larger-Hopeless policy in deadline-based scheduling, what is the probability that an arriving job is dropped?

evidence.quote: Understanding the dropping probability under DTLH is also an open problem, although the dropping probability for DIH is understood, under certain conditions; see [76].

accepted.question_text: For a queueing system with a fixed threshold t, what scheduling policy minimizes the tail probability P{Response Time > t} rather than only its asymptotic behavior as t goes to infinity?

evidence.quote: while comparing the asymptotic tail under different scheduling policies is interesting from a theoretical standpoint, it does not solve the practical question of scheduling to minimize P {Response Time > t} for a particular t; this remains an open problem.

accepted.question_text: For the M/M/k queue with setup times, where idle servers shut down and must incur setup delay before serving jobs again, can one derive a simple approximation as a function of k that captures how the response-time effect of setup diminishes in larger systems?

evidence.quote: It would be very nice to have a simple approximation for the M/M/k/setup as a function of k.

accepted.question_text: How can one analyze the M/G/k queue with setup times, where service times are general rather than exponential and idle servers may shut down and later require setup before returning to service?

evidence.quote: Finally, the M/G/k system with setup time is also a wide open problem.

needs_review.question_text_raw: In Sect. 3.4, almost everything is open when jobs have different speedup functions.

evidence.quote: In this section, we examine the important case where jobs have different speedup functions. Here, almost everything is open, but there is some intuition that can be learned from the little work that exists.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Power management raises many open questions such as when to turn servers off or on and how to schedule jobs to reduce shutdowns.

evidence.quote: This leads to a great many questions: When should one turn servers off? When should one turn them back on? How should one schedule jobs on the servers to minimize the need to turn servers off?
